Ever since Claude Code rolled out tool search (dynamic MCP loading), its built-in fetch/websearch has been getting picked over Jina Reader MCP. Turns out adding service.instruction fixes this, it's basically SEO for MCP.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_E_6i9XoAEQxZO.jpg
Quoting @yusuke_m_MU
【朗報】もしかしたら、MCP単独でSkillsに近い位置付けにできるかもしれない：MCPの最大の課題の一つだったコンテキストウィンドウの消費に対する解決策：Tool search tool がClaude Codeに導入
Claude Code が、MCP のツール説明がコンテキストの 10% 以上を使用すると判断した場合に自動検知して、必要なサーバー以外はコンテキストに入れないようになった。神すぎる。
Tool search tool が起動すると、ツールは事前ロードされず、必要と判断されたツールのみ検索経由で読み込まれるようになる。
で、ここからが重要なのが、MCPサーバーの「server instructions」です。
「instructions」はClaude に対して「いつツール検索を行うべきか」を伝える役割を果たし、Skills に近い位置づけになる。
で、MCPをそんなに使ってこなかったワイみたいな人間は、ツールのdeescriptionはしっかり書くけど、instructionsを書いてないみたいなことがある。いや、普通にあると思う。
だって、今いろんなGitHubのリモートMCPのindex.ts みに行ったら、なんと「instructions」フィールドが書かれているサーバーが1/5でしたw
というのが、サーバー全体のinstructionsは必須フィールドじゃないので、書かなくても動かせるけど、エージェントが何のサーバーがマジで分からなくなるから、これからは絶対書いた方がいい。
どこに何を書ばいいのか分からなかったら、以下の公式ドキュメントでわかるので、参考にしてみて。
ちなみにTypescript でinstructionsの記載は公式ドキュメントにないのだが、ServerOptions に instructions プロパティがある。
McpServer は第2引数として ServerOptions を受け取るので、そこに instructions を渡せばOK
よく分からなければ、このテキストをClaude Codeに渡せばやってくれます。

Seeing a lot of hype around ANE reverse engineering breakthroughs lately. Cool progress, but we benchmarked jina-v5-nano (12-layer 768d transformer) on M3 Ultra:
• MLX GPU: 4ms
• ANE hybrid (baked weights): 49ms
• ANE hybrid (dynamic weights): 236ms
ANE's value is low-power inference. It is not necessarily faster than MLX on desktop. MLX GPU does in 4ms what ANE does in 236ms on the same chip. Unified memory doesn't help when ANE must shuttle data through IOSurface kernel calls while GPU reads it directly via Metal with zero copy.
People claiming ANE beats MLX for transformer inference have simply never used MLX.

title: Han Xiao (@hxiao)
summary:
Has anyone adapted @karpathy's autoresearch for multi-objective optimization? Everything I've seen so far optimizes a single target value. would be interesting if classic techniques like multi-armed bandit end up getting reimplemented at the agent level.
Quoting @karpathy
Three days ago I left autoresearch tuning nanochat for ~2 days on depth=12 model. It found ~20 changes that improved the validation loss. I tested these changes yesterday and all of them were additive and transferred to larger (depth=24) models. Stacking up all of these changes, today I measured that the leaderboard's "Time to GPT-2" drops from 2.02 hours to 1.80 hours (~11% improvement), this will be the new leaderboard entry. So yes, these are real improvements and they make an actual difference. I am mildly surprised that my very first naive attempt already worked this well on top of what I thought was already a fairly manually well-tuned project.
This is a first for me because I am very used to doing the iterative optimization of neural network training manually. You come up with ideas, you implement them, you check if they work (better validation loss), you come up with new ideas based on that, you read some papers for inspiration, etc etc. This is the bread and butter of what I do daily for 2 decades. Seeing the agent do this entire workflow end-to-end and all by itself as it worked through approx. 700 changes autonomously is wild. It really looked at the sequence of results of experiments and used that to plan the next ones. It's not novel, ground-breaking "research" (yet), but all the adjustments are "real", I didn't find them manually previously, and they stack up and actually improved nanochat. Among the bigger things e.g.:
- It noticed an oversight that my parameterless QKnorm didn't have a scaler multiplier attached, so my attention was too diffuse. The agent found multipliers to sharpen it, pointing to future work.
- It found that the Value Embeddings really like regularization and I wasn't applying any (oops).
- It found that my banded attention was too conservative (i forgot to tune it).
- It found that AdamW betas were all messed up.
- It tuned the weight decay schedule.
- It tuned the network initialization.
This is on top of all the tuning I've already done over a good amount of time. The exact commit is here, from this "round 1" of autoresearch. I am going to kick off "round 2", and in parallel I am looking at how multiple agents can collaborate to unlock parallelism.
All LLM frontier labs will do this. It's the final boss battle. It's a lot more complex at scale of course - you don't just have a single train. py file to tune. But doing it is "just engineering" and it's going to work. You spin up a swarm of agents, you have them collaborate to tune smaller models, you promote the most promising ideas to increasingly larger scales, and humans (optionally) contribute on the edges.
And more generally, *any* metric you care about that is reasonably efficient to evaluate (or that has more efficient proxy metrics such as training a smaller network) can be autoresearched by an agent swarm. It's worth thinking about whether your problem falls into this bucket too.

using kv cache as document store is nothing new, like the old CAG paper. but with quantized kv cache and modern attention (hybrid SSM-attention, GQA, MQA, MLA), the economics are changing fast. if we solve cold-prefill speed and decoding speed, and budget GPU costs keep dropping, the future of search could be vectorless. radical, but possible.

summary:
spent some time reading the mempalace project, my honest rating: nah.
it's a handcrafted memory representation for english-only data, using the Method of Loci (palace structure) as a fancy term to farm internet likes, but in reality it's a classification system to allow prefiltered retrieval to improve recall@k. tbf, it touches some core interesting problems of agent memory like temporal dynamics, conflict resolution, knowledge graph. but the solution there is pretty premature and "symbolic", it basically tries to regex its way through every problem above, which makes the whole system brittle, symbolic, and english-only.
a few wishes:
• i wish more people realized that frontier embedding models like jina-v5, voyage, gemini already do zero-shot classification out of the box. they're trained not just for (q,d) retrieval, (d,d) similarity, but also for classification, including multi-class. you could build a mempalace by test-time scaling the embedding model into a complicated maze (or let's just call it decision tree) - no hand-coded rooms needed.
• i wish people would read up on late chunking (2024) and stop treating chunking/sliding window as some unsolved problem in 2026. long context embedding models + late chunking already solved this.
• memory representation in general feels unsolved, kinda like pre-2017 when people were still doing language modeling in wildly different ways before transformers ate everything. would love to see more work on memory representation at ICLR2026 later this month, where the R represents representation after all.
also you should probably unfollow the people promoting this project like crazy. i seriously doubt they know what they're talking about.

clean_summary:
Spent some time reading the Mempalace project; my honest rating: nah. It's a handcrafted memory representation for English-only data, using the Method of Loci as a fancy term to gain internet likes, but in reality, it's a classification system for prefiltered retrieval to improve recall@k. While it touches on interesting problems of agent memory like temporal dynamics and conflict resolution, the solution feels premature and overly symbolic, trying to regex its way through various issues, which makes the system brittle and limited to English.

I wish more people realized that frontier embedding models like Jina-v5, Voyage, and Gemini already perform zero-shot classification out of the box. They're trained not just for (q,d) retrieval and (d,d) similarity, but also for classification, including multi-class. You could build a Mempalace by scaling the embedding model into a complicated maze or decision tree—no hand-coded rooms needed.

I also wish people would read up on late chunking (2024) and stop treating chunking/sliding window as unsolved problems in 2026. Long context embedding models combined with late chunking have already addressed this. Overall, memory representation feels unsolved, similar to the pre-2017 landscape of language modeling before transformers took over. It would be great to see more work on memory representation at ICLR2026, where the 'R' represents representation after all. You should probably unfollow those promoting this project; I seriously doubt they know what they're talking about.

title: Han Xiao (@hxiao)
clean_title: Running Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with 1M context on a single L4 GPU
summary:
finally got qwen3.5-35b-a3b running at 1M context on a single L4 24GB, with 905K tokens prefilled (86% full). decoding at 9 tok/s. stuffed the entire 天龙八部 (a 1.2M-word jin yong novel, 50 chapters) into KV cache as a test. the goal is to use long-context LLM + KV cache on a budget GPU as a document store, to enbale vectorless search - no embeddings, no chunking, just LLM+raw context. L4 is the most popular budget GPU in prod, and qwen3.5-35b-a3b is the only model where 1M context can theoretically fit on 24GB VRAM. 27B dense won't work. extremely tight budget.
what it took to make it fit:
• YaRN RoPE scaling (262K training context → 1M)
• Q3_K_M quantization (20GB → 15.2GB)
• turbo3 KV cache (23GB → 4GB for 1M tokens)
• native turbo3 flash attention via Madreag/turbo3-cuda (no fp16 decompression, saves ~1.7GB that would OOM)
• ubatch=128 (compute buffer 3GB →779MB)
• slot save/restore (68-min cold prefill → 2.3s restore)
• append_to_slot patch (append query directly to cached 905K KV state, skip resending the whole novel)
• patches for qwen3.5's hybrid attention+recurrent architecture (KV truncation + slot restore were broken).
this setup gives peak vram at 96% utilization (22,052 MiB / 23,034 MiB)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFcPqwqa8AE52K3.jpg

title: Han Xiao (@hxiao)
clean_title: Shifting patterns in using agents for long-horizon tasks
summary:
seeing a pattern shift in how I use agents for long-horizon tasks in 2026 vs. how i do deep research in 2025. 2025's DR: search → read → reason → repeat until done. Everything hits the web on every loop.
but 2026 long-horizon tasks have two distinct phases.
- Phase 1: Web IO for research & planning. Search, read, reason. but the goal isn't to produce an answer directly. It's to materialize web knowledge into local files (.md/.json/.csv).
- Phase 2: Agent "mounts" the files and starts the loop. The agent reads, runs, writes against those local files only. No more web calls for grounding.
Why I cut web grounding IO in Phase 2?
• Determinism: local files are immutable snapshots. Web content shifts, 404s, hits paywalls
• Speed: filesystem reads are ms, web fetches are seconds. Agent loops need tight iteration
• Consistency: cross-checking requires operating on the same knowledge base, not fetching different versions each time
• Cost: web IO burns tokens parsing HTML noise. Local files are already clean
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGB05GyaIAAIurd.jpg
clean_summary:
I'm seeing a pattern shift in how I use agents for long-horizon tasks in 2026 compared to deep research in 2025. In 2025, the deep research process involved a cycle of search, read, reason, and repeat until done, with everything hitting the web in every loop.

However, for 2026 long-horizon tasks, there are two distinct phases. Phase 1 involves web input for research and planning, where the goal is to materialize web knowledge into local files (.md/.json/.csv) rather than producing an answer directly. Phase 2 sees the agent 'mount' these files and start the loop, reading, running, and writing against the local files only, eliminating web calls for grounding.

The reasons for cutting web grounding in Phase 2 include determinism, as local files are immutable snapshots; speed, since filesystem reads are much faster than web fetches; consistency, as cross-checking requires operating on the same knowledge base; and cost, as web input consumes tokens parsing HTML noise while local files are already clean.

Bg: I was rehearsing my talk for ICLR using Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B with my voice fingerprint. The full talk is around 5min and after 1min generation I start to gibber with a lot of stuttering and self-corrections; and at 1:20 I’m totally gone and like a broken robot. Video shows where the degeneration kicks in.
So when the autoregressive LM generates speech tokens, it hits the same repetition/degeneration wall as any text LLM. That 96-second chunk corresponds to roughly 1K speech tokens at the 12 Hz tokenizer rate. Once the LLM passes ~700-800 tokens, the attention distribution starts to collapse: same as text LLM, it falls into a repetitive loop, producing the same token patterns over and over. In the 2nd step of qwen3-tts, it uses Flow Matching that faithfully renders those looping tokens into audio, which is why we hear the stuttering and timbral drift.
Don’t play it at night.

Model training is not only distillation. IMO Anthropic should allow (even encourage) people to use Fable to supervise small-model training, for two reasons. 2026 summer is exactly the moment when people from industry in-house model labs/AI team realize they can no longer compete with frontier models like Fable, and their success story has to be written differently: instead of competing with frontier intelligence, their goal now should be using frontier intelligence to improve domain-specific models. clean_title: Using knowledge graphs to build private verifiers for agentic search
summary:
Not a fan of Knowledge Graphs, but recently I started using them more often for a surprising reason: to build non-trivial private verifiers for agentic search. For those who don't know, building a private eval set for a scaffolded LLM in 2026 is really challenging, like seriously hard. It takes a lot of effort to find a question that's non-trivial to a scaffolded LLM yet still answerable. To find those question-answer pairs, I built a knowledge graph extractor where you can throw a corpus at it, and it extracts the entity relations using qwen3.6-35b-a3b-MTP on an L4 at 70 tps (which is really good for such a low-budget GPU). Then I mark out the longest path in the graph and use it to generate challenging question-answer pairs. The idea is to find those genuinely multi-hop fact chains that are verifiable from the corpus, to stress-test the agentic search system.
